title: Standard normal distribution
summary: The standard normal distribution is N(0, 1). Its cdf satisfies Φ(0)=1/2 and Φ(-z)=1-Φ(z). Table values are used only when a question supplies them.
intuition:
The standard normal distribution is the normal law with mean 0 and variance 1, written $N(0,1)$. It is the distribution of $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma$ after a general normal variable has been standardized. Its density is even: the height at $z$ equals the height at $-z$. The cdf is $\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)$.

Symmetry does almost all of the arithmetic this lesson needs. Because the density is even and the total probability is 1,

$$
\Phi(0)=\frac{1}{2},\qquad \Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z).
$$

The right-tail probability is $P(Z\ge z)=1-\Phi(z)$. For a continuous variable the distinction between $\ge$ and $>$ does not matter. A symmetric interval has probability $P(-z\le Z\le z)=2\Phi(z)-1$. You do not need a memorised table to use these identities. If a problem needs a numerical value of $\Phi$ at a nonzero point, the problem states that value. Inventing a table entry, or treating the density height $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ as $\Phi(0)$, answers a different question from the one that was asked.

The same symmetry is why a two-sided normal probability can be read from one tail. Given $\Phi(z)$, the lower tail beyond $-z$ equals the upper tail beyond $z$, and both equal $1-\Phi(z)$.

definitions.body: A random variable $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Its mean is 0 and its variance is 1. It is the standardized form of a general normal variable.
The function $\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)$. It is continuous and strictly increasing, with limits 0 and 1 at $\pm\infty$.

A numerical value of $\Phi$ at a nonzero argument is used only when the question or the example states it. It is an input to the symmetry identities, not a number to be recalled from an unstated table.

formulas.name: Symmetry
formulas.note: Follows from an even density and total mass 1.

formulas.name: Tails and a symmetric interval
formulas.note: Use a stated value of $\Phi(z)$ when a decimal is required.

properties: The standard normal law is $N(0,1)$. Its density is even, and $\Phi(0)=1/2$.
Symmetry says $\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)$ for every $z$. The two tails beyond $z$ and beyond $-z$ are equal.
A symmetric probability is $P(|Z|\le z)=2\Phi(z)-1$. The outside probability is $2(1-\Phi(z))$.
The density at 0 is $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, which is not $\Phi(0)$. The cdf at 0 is $1/2$.
This lesson does not ask for an unstated table entry. A decimal value of $\Phi$ is either $1/2$ at 0, or a value the problem gives.

examples.title: The centre of the cdf
examples.prompt: For $Z\sim N(0,1)$, find $\Phi(0)$, $P(Z\ge 0)$, and $P(-a\le Z\le a)$ in terms of $\Phi(a)$.
steps: The mean is 0 and the density is symmetric, so half the mass is on each side of 0. Thus $\Phi(0)=P(Z\le 0)=1/2$.
The upper half is the same probability: $P(Z\ge 0)=1-\Phi(0)=1/2$. The single point 0 does not change the value.
For a positive or negative $a$, the symmetric interval has probability $\Phi(a)-\Phi(-a)=\Phi(a)-(1-\Phi(a))=2\Phi(a)-1$.
examples.answer: The value $\Phi(0)$ is $1/2$, the upper half is $1/2$, and $P(|Z|\le a)=2\Phi(a)-1$.

examples.title: A stated table value
steps: The value 0.8944 is given. Symmetry supplies the other side: $\Phi(-1.25)=1-0.8944=0.1056$.
The upper tail is the same number: $P(Z\ge 1.25)=1-\Phi(1.25)=0.1056$.
The symmetric probability is $2\times 0.8944-1=0.7888$. Equivalently, $1-2\times 0.1056=0.7888$. No further table lookup is required.

traps: Replacing $\Phi(0)$ by the density height $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$. The cdf at 0 is $1/2$. The density is a different function.
Using $\Phi(-z)=\Phi(z)$, or $\Phi(-z)=-\Phi(z)$. The identity is $\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)$. The values $\Phi(z)$ and $\Phi(-z)$ sum to 1.
Inventing a table value that the question did not give. If the stem does not state $\Phi(z)$, the expected answer is an exact symmetry consequence such as $1/2$ or an expression in a given $\Phi$.
Forgetting the factor of 2 in a two-sided probability. Given $\Phi(z)$, the central probability is $2\Phi(z)-1$, not $\Phi(z)-1/2$ left unfinished, and not $1-\Phi(z)$.

questions.stem: Z is standard normal. The value $\Phi(0)$ equals
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $1/2$.

The standard normal density is symmetric about 0, so $P(Z\le 0)=1/2$. Option D is the density at 0, not the cdf. Options B and C are the limits of $\Phi$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, not the value at 0.

questions.stem: A table gives $\Phi(0.7)=0.7580$. The value $\Phi(-0.7)$ is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $0.2420$.

Symmetry says $\Phi(-0.7)=1-\Phi(0.7)=1-0.7580=0.2420$. Option B repeats the given value and drops the complement. Option C is the central probability $2\times 0.7580-1=0.5160$, which is $P(|Z|\le 0.7)$ rather than $\Phi(-0.7)$. Option D makes the cdf negative, which a probability cannot be.

questions.stem: Z is standard normal, with cdf $\Phi$. Which of the following are true?
options: The density of $Z$ is an even function.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Symmetry of the $N(0,1)$ density gives $\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)$ and $\Phi(0)=1/2$. The two cdf values sum to 1, not to 0, so D is false. A negative cdf would not be a probability.

questions.stem: A table gives $\Phi(1.25)=0.8944$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

From the given value, $\Phi(-1.25)=1-0.8944=0.1056$, and the upper tail $P(Z\ge 1.25)$ equals that same complement. The central probability is $2\times 0.8944-1=0.7888$. Option D swaps the tails: $P(Z\le -1.25)$ is 0.1056, not 0.8944.

The answer is **6826**.

The central probability is $2\Phi(1)-1=2\times 0.8413-1=0.6826$. Multiplying by 10000 gives $2\times 8413-10000=6826$. The calculation uses only the value stated in the stem and the symmetry formula $2\Phi(1)-1$.
